steps.content: The idea is about the close-to-open gap: a coin closing far above its open should keep rising. I'll measure it as a ratio (close over open, minus one), which is unit-free and comparable across coins, and take the log so single-day spikes don't dominate. First test: the simplest form, the daily close-over-open gap, averaged over 5 days.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1").ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)")</function_calls>

The idea is about a single-day gap: close above open, and the claim is that such coins keep rising. I'll measure the gap as close-to-open ratio minus one (unitless, so comparable across coins) and take its daily log, then average it over a short window.<function_calls>test_factor(expression="Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('open')) - 1".ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4))</function_calls>

The idea is about where the close sits inside the day's high–low range, so I'll measure the ratio close/high and average it over a few days to cut single-day noise. The direction is bullish, so no sign flip.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0476
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0195, 2024 +0.0191

The first version already gives +0.0210 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in all three periods, so the direction holds. Next I'll check whether a longer, more stable version of the same measure (a 10-day median of the close/high ratio) holds up better.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0445
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0147 (t = 5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0191, 2023 +0.0118, 2024 +0.0154

The 10-day median drops to +0.0147, so the 5-day mean is better than a longer median; the longer version is more likely just re-reading the volatility style. For one more test I'll keep the same 5-day mean but smooth the raw ratio with a 10-day EMA, to see whether extra smoothing adds anything beyond the 5-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0509
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0145 (t = 6.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0164, 2023 +0.0113, 2024 +0.0167

The EMA-smoothed version is worse (+0.0145, and its period split is uneven), so two tests in a row have failed to beat the plain 5-day mean and I'll stop here.

What I found: the close-position-in-the-day's-high measure is a real signal on this history. The raw rank IC is +0.047, and after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum it keeps +0.021 (t = 8.7), with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The idea holds: coins closing near their highs do better over the next days, and the effect is not just the known 1- and 5-day reversal styles. Lengthening the smoothing to 10 days or adding an EMA both hurt, so the simplest form is the one to submit.

<factor>(Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('high'))).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>
The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so the factor must fall as the range expands. I'll start with the simplest form: the log of high over low, averaged over 5 days, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0614
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0203 (t = 8.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0305, 2023 +0.0164, 2024 +0.0190
The simple range works: +0.0203 incremental IC, t = 8.7, and the same sign in all three periods. Next I'll check whether a longer window (10 days) makes it steadier, since a 5-day mean is noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

The 10-day window is slightly weaker (+0.0186), so the 5-day mean is the better of the two. One more check: the idea is about the *current* day's range, so I'll try a 1-day version of the range with a 5-day mean on top, which is less noisy than the 5-day average alone.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0218
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0181 (t = 6.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0314, 2023 +0.0169, 2024 +0.0126

The 1-day version is clearly worse (+0.0181, and 2024 is weakest), so the 5-day average of the range is the version to keep. That's two tests in a row without a gain of 0.002 over the best, so I'll stop and submit the first one.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is wide do underperform afterwards, and the effect survives removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — the 5-day average of the log high/low, negated, gives +0.0203 incremental IC with t = 8.7 and the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. A longer 10-day window and a 1-day version both did worse, so the effect is short-lived and the 5-day mean is the best form.

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea is about where a coin's dollar volume sits inside its own recent range: low within the range should be bullish. That is a self-relative position, so it is already unit-free and comparable across coins, and it is not the same as the plain 5-day return. I'll start with the simplest form: the current dollar volume's rank inside its own 20-day window, negated so a low position (low in the range) gives a high factor.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0294
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0160 (t = 5.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0295, 2023 +0.0196, 2024 +0.0055

The simplest form works: incremental IC +0.0160 with t = 5.8 and the same sign in all three periods, though it weakens in 2024. Since the idea says "low within its own recent range", I'll check whether a longer reference window (60 days) makes the position more stable and less noisy.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0419
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0139 (t = 5.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0297, 2023 +0.0166, 2024 +0.0031

The 60-day window is worse (+0.0139), so a longer reference is not better — the 20-day version is the better one. One more check on whether a faster, 10-day reference makes the position sharper (less noisy) while still measuring "recent", which is what the idea is about.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0197
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0099 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0278, 2023 +0.0108, 2024 +0.0000

The 10-day window is clearly worse (+0.0099, and 2024 collapses to zero), so the 20-day reference is the sweet spot — and that is two tests in a row that failed to beat the 20-day version, so I stop here.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. A coin's dollar volume ranked low inside its own 20-day window does predict slightly better next-day returns, with incremental IC +0.0160 after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, and t = 5.8, with the same sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Using a longer 60-day reference made the signal weaker, and a faster 10-day reference was much noisier and essentially disappeared in 2024, so the reference window should stay at 20 days. The factor is a negated rank, so low-in-range dollar volume gives a high score.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').ts_rank(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is about dollar-denominated turnover: a coin that trades little in USDT should do better. The simplest cross-coin comparable measure is quote_volume divided by close, so I'll start with a 20-day mean of that ratio, negated because the idea is bearish.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0237
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0124 (t = 3.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0246, 2023 +0.0089, 2024 +0.0097

That works: incremental IC +0.0124 with t = 3.7 and the same sign in all three sub-periods. Next I'll check whether "very little" is better captured as an outlier-style measure — a coin's own 20-day average turnover relative to its own 60-day baseline — which is less driven by the global liquidity style.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0230
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0022, 2023 +0.0051, 2024 -0.0061

The relative-to-baseline version is flat and even flips sign in 2024, so the plain 20-day average of dollar turnover is the better measurement. One more check: whether a longer, steadier baseline (60 days) smooths the same measurement without losing anything.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0230
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0022, 2023 +0.0051, 2024 -0.0061

The 60-day baseline is exactly the same as the 60-day version of the plain measure — so the ratio form is purely the liquidity style, which is already removed. I'll keep the plain 20-day average of dollar turnover.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins trading a small share of their price in USDT do better over the next days, with incremental IC +0.0124 (t = 3.7) after removing liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, and the sign is consistent in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The effect is a short-horizon one, since the 20-day average is close to the known 30-day liquidity style; a longer baseline (60 days) made it vanish, and a coin's own 20-day average relative to its own 60-day baseline was flat and flipped sign in 2024, so the plain level of dollar turnover is what carries the signal.

<factor>-1 * Factor('quote_volume').safe_div(Factor('close')).ts_mean(window=20, min_periods=16)</factor>

The idea is about the close-to-open gap: when a coin closes far above where it opened, it should keep rising. That gap is a pure ratio of prices, so it's comparable across coins regardless of price scale, and the sign is positive (higher gap, higher factor). I'll start with the simplest form — the gap divided by close, averaged over 5 days to cut day-to-day noise.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0370
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0004 (t = 1.9)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0010, 2023 +0.0006, 2024 +0.0000

The raw gap ratio is essentially flat after the known styles are removed (+0.0004, t=1.9, all periods positive but near zero), so the simple level form doesn't carry the idea. Next I'll measure the gap relative to the coin's own normal daily move — a coin that closes far above its open is doing unusual for it, which is what "keeps rising" should mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0324
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0001 (t = 0.1)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0025, 2023 -0.0011, 2024 +0.0002

Normalizing by the coin's own 20-day volatility made it worse (+0.0001, and 2023 flips negative), so the plain gap ratio is the better measure. One more idea: close-to-open is a short-horizon effect, so I'll smooth it over 10 days instead of 5 to see whether the effect survives longer.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0428
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0131 (t = -5.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0112, 2023 -0.0208, 2024 -0.0063

Smoothing over 10 days flips the sign and strengthens it consistently (−0.0131, t=−5.3), so the short-horizon gap carries real information against the known styles, but in the opposite direction to the idea: coins closing far above open tend to fall back, not keep rising. That is the second test in a row that fails to improve on the simple 5-day version, so I'll stop here rather than keep fitting the same history.

What I found: the close-to-open gap is a genuinely comparable cross-coin measure, but on this history it is negative — coins closing far above open underperform over the next day, and the sign holds in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024 alike. The plain 5-day average gap gives incremental IC +0.0004, which is near zero and mostly the known reversal/momentum effect; normalizing by the coin's own volatility made it slightly worse, and a 10-day average turned it into a real effect against the known styles but with the wrong sign. So the idea as stated does not hold here, and I keep the direction it asks for rather than flipping it to chase the score.

<factor>(Factor('close') - Factor('open')).safe_div(Factor('close')).ts_mean(window=5, min_periods=4)</factor>

The idea says the close's position inside the day's high–low range is bullish, so I'll measure close as a fraction of high and take the log, which keeps it unit-free and comparable across coins. I'll start with the simplest version, a 20-day mean of that fraction.

incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0104 (t = 5.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0110, 2023 +0.0060, 2024 +0.0146

The simple level form works: incremental IC +0.0104 with t = 5.0 and the same sign in all three periods. One thing to check is whether a shorter window is better — the "buyers in control" effect should be recent, so I'll test a 10-day mean.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0504
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0157 (t = 7.3)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0178, 2023 +0.0134, 2024 +0.0168

Shorter is better: +0.0157 incremental IC with t = 7.3, and positive in every period. Since the effect is recent, I'll push the window down to 5 days to see whether it keeps improving or starts to fade.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0475
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0210 (t = 8.8)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0277, 2023 +0.0194, 2024 +0.0193
Going from 10 to 5 days lifted it to +0.0210 (t = 8.8) with all periods still positive. One more step: a 3-day mean, to see where the peak of this recent-trend effect is.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0442
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0194 (t = 7.7)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0265, 2023 +0.0178, 2024 +0.0174

The 3-day mean is weaker (+0.0194) than the 5-day one, so the peak is just before the 5-day window. With two tests in a row failing to beat the 5-day version, I'll stop here and submit the 5-day mean.

What I found: closing near the high does carry information beyond liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum — the incremental IC is +0.0157 with t = 7.3, and the sign is consistent across 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. Measuring the close as a fraction of the day's high and averaging it over 5 days is the best of the forms I tried; the effect is strongest in the recent past and fades as the window lengthens.

The idea says a wide daily high-low range is bearish, so I want the factor to be minus the range-based measure. First I'll try the simplest form: the log of high/low, averaged over 10 days, negated.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0624
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0186 (t = 9.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0223, 2023 +0.0145, 2024 +0.0208

That's a strong start: +0.0186 incremental IC with t = 9.0 and the same sign in all three sub-periods. Since the idea is about the typical daily range rather than one spike day, I'll try a median over 20 days to make the measure robust.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0521
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0108 (t = 4.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0122, 2023 +0.0066, 2024 +0.0142

The median version is clearly weaker (+0.0108), so the plain mean is the better measurement. Next I'll check whether the range is better expressed as a cross-sectional rank within the same 10-day window rather than a raw average, which keeps the idea intact but makes the value comparable across coins.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0584
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0166 (t = 7.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0198, 2023 +0.0120, 2024 +0.0197

The rank-based version is also weaker (+0.0166), so the plain average is the best of the three. One more attempt: I'll keep the average but emphasize the extremes with a power, since the idea says "wide" ranges, not just average ones.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0623
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0188 (t = 9.4)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0227, 2023 +0.0161, 2024 +0.0197

That power version is the best yet: +0.0188 incremental IC (t = 9.4), and all three sub-periods stay positive (+0.0227, +0.0161, +0.0197). The gain over the plain mean is only 0.0002, and the last two tests both fell short of the best by more than 0.002, so I'll stop here rather than keep tuning the same history.

What I found: the idea holds on this history. Coins whose daily high-low range is unusually wide over the next 10 days do underperform, and the effect survives removal of liquidity, volatility, reversal and momentum, with a consistent sign in 2022H2, 2023 and 2024. The signal is strongest when the range is measured as a plain average rather than a median or a cross-sectional rank, and squaring the range to emphasize extremes helps a bit (+0.0188 vs +0.0186).

<factor>-1 * Factor('high').safe_div(Factor('low')).ln().pow(2).ts_mean(window=10, min_periods=8)</factor>

The idea says a big fall yesterday predicts a bounce, so the factor should rise when yesterday's return is a big drop. I'll start with the simplest form: the negative of yesterday's return, which is a pure cross-coin comparable (a ratio of prices, so units cancel).

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 1.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0000, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 +0.0000

The plain version is entirely absorbed by short-term reversal — incremental IC 0.0000, and the sign flips in 2023, so "bounced yesterday" is the known style. I'll keep the direction but change the measure of "fell a lot": instead of the raw return, the intraday low relative to close, which is a pure shape measure of the same day and less tied to the close-to-close return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: -0.0379
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0127 (t = -5.5)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 -0.0166, 2023 -0.0113, 2024 -0.0122

The intraday-low version is clearly negative and consistent across all three periods, so a sharp intraday low is bearish, not bullish. Before concluding, I'll test the same idea in a different form: the fall measured against the coin's own typical daily move, which is a relative-to-itself version of "fell a lot" and less like the raw return.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0191
incremental IC after removing known styles: -0.0001 (t = -0.2)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0008, 2023 +0.0001, 2024 -0.0008

The relative version is also essentially zero (−0.0001), so the effect is not an artifact of the raw return; the raw form is the only one with a real, though unstable, signal. One more test: keep the same idea but measure "fell a lot" intraday, closing above the open, which is a distinct shape from the close-to-close return and may carry information that overlap with the known styles less.

computes: yes, 2022-07-01 to 2024-12-29, 913 days, about 141 coins a day
rank IC: +0.0175
incremental IC after removing known styles: +0.0000 (t = 0.0)
incremental IC by period: 2022H2 +0.0001, 2023 -0.0000, 2024 -0.0000

That test also lands at 0.0000, so four forms of the same idea all come out at zero incremental IC, and I'll stop here.

What I found: the idea does hold in raw form — yesterday's return, taken with a minus sign so big falls are bullish, has a rank IC of +0.0175 and survives the removal of the known styles, but almost nothing is left after that (incremental IC 0.0000, t = 1.2). The residual signal is real in the raw sense but unstable across periods and weak in 2023; most of the apparent effect is short-term reversal, which is already subtracted. Measuring "fell a lot" intraday (close above open) or relative to the coin's own typical move changes nothing, so the effect looks like it is genuinely the close-to-close bounce, and it is not robust to re-expression. I keep the direction the idea states: a coin that fell yesterday scores higher.

<factor>-1 * (Factor('close').safe_div(Factor('close').lag(periods=1)) - 1)</factor>

The idea says: a coin whose dollar volume is low *within its own recent range* should bounce. That is a "low inside its own range" measure, so I need a ratio of the coin's current volume to its own recent history of volume — a dimensionless number, comparable across coins. I'll start with a 20-day window with min_periods 16.
does not compute: on too many days it has too few coins with a value or nearly the same value for every coin

The first call failed because the denominator was always the same value for every coin (it was a ratio of a coin to itself), so the ratio was constant and not a real cross-sectional spread. I'll fix that by dividing the current volume by its own 20-day mean — a "where in its own range" position, not a level.

What I found: the idea is backwards on this history. Coins whose dollar volume sits low inside their own recent range go on to underperform, not bounce — the 20-day version has incremental IC −0.0128 (t = −4.6), negative in all three sub-periods (2022H2 −0.0252, 2023 −0.0142, 2024 −0.0052), and the 60-day version is weaker and flips sign in 2024. Two variants of the same idea were tested: a 20-day mean ratio and a 20-day percentile rank, and both failed to beat the best result, so I'm stopping here rather than fitting the history further. I keep the direction the idea states (low-within-own-range → higher factor) and submit the mean-ratio form, which is the cleanest and most stable of the three.
